sources.citation: Mallikarjun, B. 1993. A Descriptive Analysis of Yerava. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. 382 pp. (archive.org dli.language.0068, Digital Library of India scan with text)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, HathiTrust search-only; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL4719.5.Y47 M35 1993)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL4719.5.Y47 M35 1993
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. II Phonology (pp. 51-84) lists 6 suprasegmental phonemes = 3 junctures (+, -, #) and 3 terminal contours (rising, falling, level) (2.2.2, 2.3.2, 2.4.2 pp. 53-61); syllable-type section 2.8 (pp. 78-84) is purely CV-templatic. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the book (a full-text search for stress/accent). Describes Paniya Yerava speech of Kodagu.

sources.citation: Nair, Ravi Sankar S. 2013. Tribal Languages of Kerala. Language in India 13(7) (July 2013), 58 pp; Adiya sketch pp. 3-7
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Only segmental correspondences with Malayalam (M akattu -> Adiya akaattu, akalam -> akeela: Malayalam short vowels 'frequently replaced by long vowels' in the second syllable; final -u fully rounded; l -> v; v -> b).

sources.citation: Menon, T. Madhava (chief ed.) 1996. The Encyclopaedia of Dravidian Tribes, Vol. II. Thiruvananthapuram: International School of Dravidian Linguistics. Articles 'ADIYA LANGUAGE' and 'YERAVA LANGUAGE' (pp. 378-380) (archive.org aclcpl00000220a778 scanned text)
sources.note: Nothing on stress. 'YERAVA LANGUAGE' summarises Mallikarjun 1993 (vowel/consonant counts, '6 suprasegmentals'); 'ADIYA LANGUAGE' repeats the Malayalam-Adiya vowel-length correspondences. States (p. 380) that Pani(ya) Yerava speech 'seems to be the same as that of the Paniya, while that of the Panjiri is identical with the Adiya of Wayanad'.
